DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: //www.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 59 s. 2022 June 30, 2022 MR. ALLEN A. CAPUYAN Chairperson National Commission on Indigenous Peoples Dear Chairperson Capuyan: This refers to your earlier letter requesting this Department's opinion on the following: (1) proposal of Indigenous Peoples (IP) communities on the need for a district representation for IPMR in local legislative councils; and (2) proper interpretation on the prohibition on government workers in engaging in partisan political activity in relation to Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representatives (IPMRs). We shall address the foregoing issues in seriatim On the first issue, as premised, the proposed expansion of IPMR in local legislative councils stemmed from the observation that the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act does not expressly limit the number of IP representative to only one legislative council. Accordingly, an addendum to Section 6 of Administrative Order (AO) No. 1 series of 2021 is being proposed, thus: "Section 6. Coverage Xxx c. In the Sangguniang Panlalawigan and Sangguniang Panglungsod (sic), where there are two (2) or more legislative districts, the LGU may allow one (1) IP representative per district to be selected from the qualified ICCs/IPs within the district; In the Sangguniang Barangay and Sangguniang Bayan, where there are two (2) or more qualified ICCs/lPs in accordance with paragraphs a and b above, the concerned LGU may allow at least two (2) IP representative in the Sanggunian. Xxx Xxx" Insofar as the representation of IP communities in local legislative councils in concerned, Sections 446, 457, and 467 of the Local Government Code of 1991 (Republic Act No. 7160) insofar as it provides in addition to the composition of the sanggunians, one (1) representative from other sectors including the indigenous Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

cultural communities, have been amended by Republic Act No. 8371 , otherwise known as "The Indigenous Peoples Rights Act of 1997" The aforesaid law recognizes the policy of the State in affording the indigenous people communities adequate representations in the local government sanggunian at all levels (DILG Legal Opinion No. I series of 2015, dated 12 January 2015). Notably, the aforesaid law did not specifically provide the mechanisms for the mandatory representation of IP in local legislative councils, much less expressly provide therein the number of IP representatives in local legislative councils. However, as we manifested in our previous Opinion, as aforecited, RA 8371 gives prerogatives to NCIP to review and assess the conditions of ICCs/lPs including existing laws and policies pertinent thereto and to propose relevant laws and policies to address their role in national developmentl. Accordingly, this level submits that the NCIP may amend the policy as contemplated herein, which in effect allow the representation of more than one IP in the concerned sanggunian, (i) one IP representative per district where there are two or more legislative districts in the Sangguniang PanlaIawigan/PanIungsod; and (ii) where there are two (2) or more qualified ICCs/lPs, the Sangguniang Barangay/Bayan may allow at least two representatives. To our mind, the proposed addendum will ensure maximum participation of IP in the local legislative councils. The same is consistent with Section 2 of Republic Act No. 8371 (The Indigenous Peoples Rights Act of 1997) when it expressly provides that "The State recognizes its obligations to respond to the strong expression of the ICCs/IPs for cultural integrity by assuring maximum ICC/IP participation in the direction of education, health, as well as other services of ICCs/lPs, in order to render such services more responsive to the needs and desires of these communities. " Be that as it may, Section 1 1 of NCIP AO No. 0012, Series of 2009 states that for LGUs with more than one (I) ICCs/lPs residing within its jurisdiction, all ICCs/lPs tribes in said LGU may agree on a term-sharing agreements based on population ratio, or on whatever local arrangement they may deem suited and applicable to address the cultural peculiarities in the LGU. The same should be reconciled with the proposed amendment to properly guide the concerned sanggunians on ICCs/lPs representation, and to avoid further conflict regarding the matter. As to the second issue, it may not be amiss to note that IPMRs are, for all intents and purposes, deemed to be elective officials. This Department consistently considers the sectoral representatives such as IPMRs as ex-officio members (DILG Legal Opinion No. 01, series of 2015) akin to an elective office. Relative thereto, the directive of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) En- Banc in its Minute Resolution No. 22-0198 dated March 2, 2022 finds application. Pertinent portion of which reads: 1 Section 44(b), RA No. 8371 2 Entitled, "NATIONAL GUIDELINES FOR THE MANDATORY REPRESENTATION OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLES IN LOCAL LEGISLATIVE COUNCILS" Page 2 of 3 "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

"The intent of both Congress and the framers of our Constitution to limit the participation of civil service officers and employees in partisan political activities is too plain to be mistaken. But Section 2(4), Article IX-B of the 1987 Constitution and the implementing statutes apply only to civil servants holding apolitical offices. Stated differently, the constitutional ban does not cover elected officials, notwithstanding the fact that '[t]he civil service embraces all branches, subdivisions instrumentalities, and agencies of the Government, including government-owned or controlled corporations with original charters. This is because elected public officials, by the very nature of their office, engage in partisan political activities almost all year round, even outside of the campaign period. Political partisanship is the inevitable essence of a political office, elective positions included. Section 261 (i) clearly excepted, without qualification, those who are holding political offices. Quinto, likewise, did not quality who among the elected officials is not covered by the constitutional ban which is implemented by Section 261 (i), among other statutes." Premises considered, we are of the view that IPMRs are excepted from the prohibition against engaging in electioneering or partisan political activities. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you.
